title: Filesystem is full
summary: Writes fail with no space left. Find what is consuming it before deleting anything.

steps.title: See which filesystem is actually full
steps.look: The Use% column, and note the mount point. A full /var is a very different problem from a full /home.

signals.means: That filesystem is completely full.
Container or snap storage, not the host's own data.

steps.title: Check inodes, because df can lie
steps.look: Space free but IUse% at 100 means inode exhaustion. The error is identical but the fix is completely different.

steps.title: Find the largest directories
steps.look: The -x keeps it on one filesystem so you are not misled by other mounts. Work downward from the largest entry.

steps.title: Find space held by deleted but still-open files
steps.look: A deleted file held open by a running process still occupies disk. This explains the case where du shows far less than df.

signals.means: Space is held by a deleted file still open. Restarting that process releases it.

causes.cause: Log files grew without rotation.
causes.fix: Truncate with : > file rather than deleting, so the open handle stays valid. Then fix logrotate.

causes.cause: A process holds a deleted file open.
causes.fix: Restart that process. No amount of deleting will reclaim the space otherwise.

causes.cause: Inodes exhausted by many small files.
causes.fix: Find the directory with the most entries and clear it. Often a session or cache directory.

causes.cause: Container images and layers.
causes.fix: Prune the container runtime's storage, with a time filter rather than wholesale.

verify: df shows meaningful free space.
The write that was failing now succeeds.
Rotation or cleanup is configured so it does not recur.
escalate: Whether any deleted files are still held open

title: Address already in use
summary: A service will not start because something already holds its port.

steps.title: Find what is listening
steps.look: The process name and PID in the last column. Without sudo you will not see the owner for another user's process.

signals.means: A process holds it. The name and PID are in the parentheses.
Nothing is listening, so the failure is something else.

steps.title: Check whether it is bound on a different interface
steps.look: 0.0.0.0 versus 127.0.0.1 versus a specific IP. Two processes can bind the same port on different addresses, which looks contradictory until you see this.

steps.title: Check for a socket stuck in TIME_WAIT
steps.look: TIME_WAIT entries without a listener mean the old socket has not been released. SO_REUSEADDR in the application is the correct fix, not waiting.

steps.title: Stop the process holding the port
steps.look: Re-run ss to confirm the port is free before starting your service.
steps.note: Terminates the process. If it is a production service, its clients drop immediately. Confirm what the PID actually is with ps before running this, and prefer the service manager's stop command so it shuts down cleanly.

causes.cause: Another process is bound to the port.
causes.fix: Stop it through its service manager, or configure your service to use a different port.

causes.cause: An old socket has not been released.
causes.fix: Enable SO_REUSEADDR in the application. Waiting works but is not a fix.

causes.cause: Bound to a specific address that overlaps your wildcard bind.
causes.fix: Bind to a specific address instead of 0.0.0.0.

causes.cause: A systemd socket unit holds the port.
causes.fix: Stop the .socket unit, not just the .service.

verify: The service starts and is listening.
ss shows it as the owner of the port.
escalate: Whether it is managed by systemd

title: systemd service will not start
summary: systemctl start fails or the unit restarts in a loop. The journal has the real reason.

steps.title: Read the unit's current state and last lines
steps.look: The Active line and the exit status. 'code=exited status=N' is the application's own exit code and the most useful number on the screen.

signals.means: systemd could not execute the binary. Wrong path, or not executable.
WorkingDirectory does not exist.
The configured User does not exist.
It started but never signalled readiness in time.

steps.title: Read the journal for this unit's last start
steps.look: The application's own output. systemctl status truncates; this does not.

steps.title: Validate the unit file itself
steps.look: Syntax problems and unresolvable references that status will never mention.

steps.title: Reload systemd after editing a unit
steps.look: No output means success. Start the unit again afterwards.
steps.note: Re-reads all unit files. Running services are not restarted and nothing is interrupted, but forgetting this after an edit means systemd keeps using the old definition and your change appears to do nothing.

causes.cause: ExecStart points at something that cannot be executed.
causes.fix: Use an absolute path and check the execute bit. systemd does not use your shell's PATH.

causes.cause: The User directive names an account that does not exist.
causes.fix: Create the user or correct the name.

causes.cause: WorkingDirectory does not exist.
causes.fix: Create it, or remove the directive.

causes.cause: Type=notify or forking, but the process does not behave that way.
causes.fix: Use Type=simple for a process that stays in the foreground. This mismatch causes start timeouts constantly.

causes.cause: The unit file was edited without a daemon-reload.
causes.fix: Run systemctl daemon-reload after every unit file change.

verify: systemctl status shows active and running.
It survives a reboot if it is enabled.
The journal shows a clean startup.
escalate: journalctl for the last start attempt

title: Load average is high and the box feels slow
summary: High load can mean CPU, disk wait or thread explosion. They look identical at first and need different fixes.

steps.title: Separate CPU from I/O wait
steps.look: The %Cpu line. High us means real computation; high wa means processes blocked on disk; high sy means kernel overhead, often context switching.

signals.means: Significant I/O wait. The disk, not the CPU, is the bottleneck.
Steal time. The hypervisor is taking cycles; this is a noisy-neighbour problem.

steps.title: Compare load against core count
steps.look: Load equal to core count is fully busy, not broken. Load at several times the core count is where queuing hurts.

steps.title: Find the top consumers
steps.look: The elapsed time column matters as much as the CPU column. A process at 100% for three seconds is normal; for three hours it is not.

steps.title: Check whether processes are blocked rather than running
steps.look: State D is uninterruptible sleep, almost always disk or NFS. Load counts these, which is why a box can show high load with idle CPUs.

causes.cause: Processes are blocked on disk.
causes.fix: Find the process doing the I/O. The CPU is not the constraint and adding cores will not help.

causes.cause: One process is consuming the CPU.
causes.fix: Identify it from the elapsed time. Restart or throttle it depending on what it is.

causes.cause: A large number of threads or processes.
causes.fix: Check the thread count. An unbounded worker pool is a common cause.

causes.cause: The hypervisor is taking CPU time.
causes.fix: This is not fixable from inside the guest. Raise it with the platform owner.

causes.cause: Load is roughly equal to core count under real work.
causes.fix: Nothing is wrong. Measure response time rather than load average.

verify: Load is proportional to core count under normal work.
Response times are acceptable.
The specific contributor was identified, not just observed.
escalate: Top processes by CPU with elapsed time

title: SSH permission denied (publickey)
summary: The server rejected your key. Verbose output names the exact reason.

steps.title: Run with verbose output and read which keys were offered
steps.look: Which keys the client offered and which methods the server accepts. If your key was never offered, the problem is local, not on the server.

signals.means: The key was offered and rejected. The problem is server-side authorization.
The key file does not exist at the path the client expects.
The private key is readable by others, so ssh refuses to use it.

steps.title: Check local key permissions
steps.look: The private key must be 600 and the directory 700. ssh silently refuses keys that are more permissive.

steps.title: Confirm which key the client will use for this host
steps.look: The resolved config. A ~/.ssh/config entry may be pointing at a different key than you assume.

steps.title: Check the server side if you have another way in
steps.look: sshd states the precise reason, including permission problems on the remote authorized_keys file, which the client can never see.

causes.cause: The public key is not in the remote authorized_keys.
causes.fix: Add it. Confirm you copied the .pub file, not the private key.

causes.cause: Local private key permissions are too open.
causes.fix: chmod 600 on the key and 700 on ~/.ssh.

causes.cause: The remote ~/.ssh or authorized_keys is group-writable.
causes.fix: chmod 700 ~/.ssh and 600 authorized_keys on the server. sshd refuses them otherwise and logs the reason.

causes.cause: The key file is not where the client looks.
causes.fix: Point at it with -i, or add an IdentityFile entry to ~/.ssh/config.

causes.cause: Correct key, wrong username.
causes.fix: Cloud images each have their own default user. ubuntu, ec2-user and admin are not interchangeable.

verify: SSH connects without a password prompt.
It works from a fresh shell, not only with an explicit -i flag.
escalate: ssh -vvv output around the authentication attempt
auth.log from the server if reachable

title: Process was killed by the OOM killer
summary: A process vanished with no error. The kernel killed it to reclaim memory.

steps.title: Confirm the kernel did it
steps.look: The timestamp, the process name and its RSS at the moment of death. This is definitive; without it you are only guessing.

signals.means: Confirmed. The kernel chose this process as the victim.
A cgroup limit, not the whole host. Only that container or unit was constrained.

steps.title: See the current memory picture
steps.look: available, not free. Linux uses free memory for cache by design, so a low free number is normal and not a problem.

steps.title: Find the current biggest consumers
steps.look: RSS in kilobytes. Compare the top entry against total memory to see whether one process dominates.

steps.title: Check what the kernel would kill next
steps.cmd: for p in $(pgrep {process}); do echo "$p $(cat /proc/$p/oom_score)"; done
steps.look: Higher score means more likely to be chosen. Useful for predicting the next victim before it happens.

causes.cause: The host ran out of memory.
causes.fix: Reduce the workload, add memory, or set limits so one process cannot take everything.

causes.cause: A container or systemd unit hit its own limit.
causes.fix: Raise MemoryMax or the container limit, having measured the real requirement first.

causes.cause: No swap, so there is no buffer before the killer runs.
causes.fix: A small swap file gives the kernel room to reclaim before killing. Not a substitute for enough RAM.

causes.cause: Memory grows without bound.
causes.fix: Profile the process. The OOM killer is a symptom, not the problem.

verify: The process stays running through a full workload cycle.
free shows headroom in available.
A limit exists so one process cannot take the whole host.

title: Cron job never runs
summary: The entry is in the crontab but nothing happens. Almost always environment or the schedule itself.

steps.title: Confirm cron attempted to run it
steps.look: A line for your job means cron fired and the problem is in the script. No line at all means cron never scheduled it.

signals.means: Cron ran it. The failure is inside the command.
Cron never fired it.
It ran and produced output cron could not mail. The output is being lost.

steps.title: Check the entry is in the crontab you think
steps.look: User crontabs and /etc/crontab are separate. The system file has an extra user field; the user crontab does not, and putting a user field in a user crontab breaks the line silently.

steps.title: Check the schedule expression is what you intend
steps.cmd: echo 'Read the five fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week'
steps.look: Setting both day-of-month and day-of-week means OR, not AND, which surprises almost everyone. A job set for the 1st and Monday runs on both.

steps.title: Run the command in cron's own environment
steps.look: env -i strips the environment the way cron does. A script that works in your shell and fails here has a PATH problem, which is the single most common cause.

causes.cause: Cron ran it and it failed.
causes.fix: Redirect output to a file in the crontab line so the failure is visible.

causes.cause: Cron's PATH is minimal.
causes.fix: Use absolute paths for every binary, or set PATH at the top of the crontab.

causes.cause: Output goes to mail and there is no mail transfer agent.
causes.fix: Append >> /var/log/myjob.log 2>&1 to the crontab line.

causes.cause: An unescaped % in the command.
causes.fix: In crontab, % means newline. Escape it as \% — date format strings hit this constantly.

causes.cause: The crontab file has no trailing newline.
causes.fix: The last line is ignored without one. Always edit with crontab -e.

causes.cause: Entry is in a different crontab than the one running.
causes.fix: Check both the user crontab and /etc/cron.d.

verify: The job appears in syslog at the expected time.
Its output lands in a log file.
It works from a clean environment, not just your shell.
escalate: Syslog CRON lines for the job

title: Too many open files
summary: A process hits its file descriptor limit. Sockets count as files, so busy servers hit this without touching disk.

steps.title: Read the limit the running process actually has
steps.look: The running process's real limit, which is what matters. Your shell's ulimit is irrelevant to a process started by systemd.

steps.title: Count how many it currently holds
steps.look: Compare against the soft limit. Close to it under normal load means the limit is too low; growing steadily means a leak.

steps.title: See what kind of descriptors they are
steps.cmd: ls -l /proc/{pid}/fd | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
steps.look: Mostly sockets points at connection handling. Many copies of one file points at a leak in the code.

signals.means: Sockets dominate. Connection churn or unclosed connections.
Deleted files still held open. Also consuming disk.

steps.title: Check the system-wide ceiling too
steps.look: The first number in file-nr is allocated across the whole system. Near file-max means a host-wide limit rather than a per-process one.

causes.cause: The per-process limit is below what the workload needs.
causes.fix: Raise LimitNOFILE in the systemd unit. limits.conf does not apply to systemd services, which catches people out.

causes.cause: Connections are not being closed.
causes.fix: Check for missing close calls or an unbounded connection pool.

causes.cause: The process opens files and never closes them.
causes.fix: Deleted-but-open entries are a strong signal. Fix the code; raising the limit only delays it.

causes.cause: The host-wide maximum is reached.
causes.fix: Raise fs.file-max, and find which process is consuming them.

causes.cause: The limit was set in the wrong file.
causes.fix: For systemd services use LimitNOFILE in the unit. For login shells use limits.conf.

verify: The process runs without hitting the limit under normal load.
The descriptor count is stable rather than growing.
The limit is set where the service actually reads it.

title: System clock is wrong or drifting
summary: Certificate errors, token rejections and confusing log ordering all trace back to clock skew.

steps.title: Check the sync status
steps.look: System clock synchronized and the NTP service state. Both must be yes and active; either one alone is not enough.

signals.means: Not synchronised. The service is not working.
No time daemon is running at all.
Hardware clock in local time, which causes drift on dual-boot machines.

steps.title: Check how far off it actually is
steps.look: System time offset in seconds. Kerberos and many token systems reject anything beyond about five minutes.

steps.title: Check the daemon can reach its sources
steps.look: A caret and asterisk marks the selected source. All sources unreachable means egress to UDP 123 is blocked.

steps.title: Force an immediate step correction
steps.look: chronyc tracking shows the offset near zero afterwards.
steps.note: Jumps the clock rather than slewing it gradually. A backward jump can confuse applications that assume time only moves forward, and databases in particular dislike it. Prefer letting chrony slew unless the offset is too large to correct that way.

causes.cause: No time synchronisation service is running.
causes.fix: Install and enable chrony. Do not run two time daemons together.

causes.cause: The daemon runs but cannot sync.
causes.fix: Check the sources. UDP 123 egress is often blocked by default in cloud security groups.

causes.cause: NTP traffic cannot leave the host.
causes.fix: Allow UDP 123, or point at an internal NTP server.

causes.cause: The hardware clock is in local time.
causes.fix: Set it to UTC. Dual-boot machines with Windows commonly get this wrong.

causes.cause: The VM was suspended and resumed.
causes.fix: The guest agent normally corrects this. Check it is installed and running.

verify: timedatectl reports synchronised.
The offset is small and stable.
Certificate and token errors have stopped.

title: Could not get lock on the package manager
summary: apt or yum refuses to run because another process holds the lock.

steps.title: Find which process holds the lock
steps.look: The process name and PID. unattended-upgrades appearing here is normal on a freshly booted machine and will finish on its own.

signals.means: Automatic updates are running. Wait rather than intervene.
Another apt session. Possibly your own in a different terminal.
Nothing holds it. The lock is stale.

steps.title: Check whether automatic updates are active
steps.look: Active means waiting is correct. This typically clears within a few minutes of boot.

steps.title: Check whether dpkg was interrupted
steps.look: Packages left half-configured by an interrupted run. These must be resolved before anything else will work.

steps.title: Repair an interrupted installation
steps.look: No output means all packages are consistent. Retry the original command afterwards.
steps.note: Finishes configuring every half-installed package. Services belonging to those packages may restart as part of it, so on a production host do this in a maintenance window. It does not remove anything.

causes.cause: Automatic updates hold the lock.
causes.fix: Wait. Killing it mid-transaction leaves the package database inconsistent.

causes.cause: Another apt session is open.
causes.fix: Finish or close it. Check other terminals and any running automation.

causes.cause: The lock file remains after a killed process.
causes.fix: Only after confirming nothing holds it, remove the lock files and run dpkg --configure -a.

causes.cause: A previous run was interrupted.
causes.fix: dpkg --configure -a repairs it. Nothing else will proceed until this is done.

causes.cause: cloud-init is still running on a new instance.
causes.fix: Wait for it to finish. It installs packages during first boot.

verify: The package command completes.
dpkg --audit reports nothing.
No transaction was killed mid-way.

title: sudo fails or asks for an unexpected password
summary: Privilege escalation is refused, or a script that expects passwordless sudo hangs waiting for input.
aliases: user is not in the sudoers file

steps.title: Check what the user is permitted to do
steps.look: The exact rules that apply. NOPASSWD must appear for the specific command if automation is to run unattended.

signals.means: No sudo rule applies to this user at all.
Passwordless is configured. Check it covers the command you are running.
Full sudo, but a password is required.

steps.title: Check group membership
steps.look: sudo or wheel in the group list, depending on the distribution. A group added during the current session does not apply until a new login.

steps.title: Validate the sudoers configuration parses
steps.look: A syntax error anywhere in sudoers or sudoers.d can disable sudo entirely, which is why visudo exists.

steps.title: Check the drop-in files, which override the main file
steps.look: Later files override earlier ones. A file with the wrong permissions or a dot in its name is ignored silently, which is a very common cause.

causes.cause: The user has no sudo rule.
causes.fix: Add them to the sudo or wheel group, or create a drop-in file. Always edit with visudo.

causes.cause: Group membership was added during the current session.
causes.fix: Log out and back in. Group membership is fixed at login.

causes.cause: A password is required and automation cannot supply one.
causes.fix: Add a NOPASSWD rule scoped to the specific commands, never to ALL.

causes.cause: NOPASSWD covers different commands.
causes.fix: The path must match exactly, including arguments if specified.

causes.cause: A sudoers.d file is ignored.
causes.fix: It must be mode 0440 and its name must contain no dot or tilde. sudo says nothing when it skips a file.

causes.cause: sudoers has a syntax error.
causes.fix: visudo -c names the line. If sudo is already broken you need root or single-user mode.

verify: sudo -l shows the intended permissions.
The command runs without an unexpected prompt.
visudo -c reports no errors.

title: Certificate verification failed
summary: TLS connections fail. Expiry, an untrusted issuer and a hostname mismatch all look similar at first.

steps.title: Read the certificate the server presents
steps.look: notAfter, the subject and the issuer. These three answer expiry, hostname and trust in one command.

signals.means: Compare the date against now. An expired certificate is the simplest case.
Self-signed, so no public CA vouches for it.

steps.title: Read the verification result specifically
steps.look: The verify return code and its text. Code 10 is expired, 18 is self-signed, 20 is an unobtainable issuer, and each has a different fix.

signals.means: Expired.
Self-signed or a self-signed root in the chain.
The chain is incomplete or the CA is not trusted.

steps.title: Check the hostname matches the certificate
steps.cmd: openssl s_client -connect {host}:{port} -servername {host} < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -A2 'Subject Alternative Name'
steps.look: The name you connect to must appear in the SAN list. The Common Name is no longer used by modern clients at all.

steps.title: Check the host's own trust store is current
steps.look: An old container image can carry a trust store predating a CA change, which makes a perfectly valid certificate fail.

causes.cause: The certificate has expired.
causes.fix: Renew it. If renewal is automated, find out why it stopped rather than only renewing by hand.

causes.cause: The server does not send intermediates.
causes.fix: Configure the full chain. Browsers often fetch missing intermediates; command-line clients do not, which is why it works in a browser and fails in a script.

causes.cause: Self-signed or issued by a private CA.
causes.fix: Add the CA to the trust store. Never disable verification to make it pass.

causes.cause: The name is not in the SAN list.
causes.fix: Reissue with the correct names. CN alone is ignored by modern clients.

causes.cause: The client's CA bundle is out of date.
causes.fix: Update ca-certificates. Old base images are the usual cause.

causes.cause: The host clock is wrong, so a valid certificate appears not yet valid.
causes.fix: Follow the time drift runbook.

verify: openssl reports verify return code 0.
The application connects without disabling verification.
Renewal is automated with monitoring on expiry.
escalate: Whether the SAN list covers the hostname

title: Read-only file system
summary: Writes fail even as root. The filesystem was remounted read-only, usually to protect it.

steps.title: Confirm the mount is read-only
steps.look: The (ro flag in the options. Present means read-only, and something caused that.

signals.means: Mounted read-only.

steps.title: Check whether the kernel remounted it after an error
steps.cmd: sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'remount|read-only|EXT4-fs error|I/O error' | tail -15
steps.look: The kernel remounts read-only after filesystem errors to prevent further damage. That is a hardware or corruption signal, not a configuration one.

signals.means: Filesystem or disk errors forced the remount. Do not simply remount it writable.
The kernel deliberately protected the filesystem.

steps.title: Check whether fstab declares it read-only
steps.look: An ro option in fstab means it was mounted this way intentionally, which is entirely different from an error-driven remount.

steps.title: Check the disk's own health
steps.look: Failing hardware behind a read-only remount means the priority is getting data off, not fixing the mount.

causes.cause: The kernel remounted after filesystem errors.
causes.fix: Do not force it writable. Take a backup, then run fsck from a live environment or rescue boot.

causes.cause: fstab declares it read-only.
causes.fix: Someone chose this. Find out why before changing it.

causes.cause: The underlying disk is failing.
causes.fix: Recover data first. A writable remount on failing hardware makes things worse.

causes.cause: A container's root filesystem is read-only by design.
causes.fix: Mount a writable volume where writes are needed. Keep the rootfs read-only.

causes.cause: The filesystem filled and then errored.
causes.fix: Follow the disk-full runbook after fsck.

verify: Writes succeed.
dmesg shows no new filesystem errors.
If it was an error, the cause was found rather than bypassed.
escalate: The mount line with its options

title: Process will not terminate
summary: kill has no effect. The process is in an uninterruptible state or being restarted.

steps.title: Check the process state
steps.look: State D means uninterruptible sleep and no signal will reach it. State Z means it is already dead and only the exit status remains.

signals.means: Uninterruptible sleep, usually blocked on I/O. Signals are queued, not delivered.
A zombie. Already dead; the parent has not reaped it.

steps.title: Find what it is blocked on
steps.look: The kernel function it is waiting in. NFS and failing block devices are the classic causes of a permanent D state.

steps.title: Check whether a supervisor restarts it
steps.look: If systemd or another supervisor owns it, killing the process just makes it come back. Stop the unit instead.

steps.title: Stop it through its supervisor
steps.look: ps shows the process gone and not replaced by a new PID.
steps.note: Stops the service cleanly and prevents the automatic restart. The service is unavailable until started again, so on a production host arrange cover first. This is the correct approach; killing a supervised PID only triggers a restart.

causes.cause: The process is in D state on blocked I/O.
causes.fix: Signals cannot reach it. Fix the I/O: a hung NFS mount or a failing disk. It exits once the I/O completes or errors.

causes.cause: It is already dead.
causes.fix: Zombies consume only a process table entry. Fix or restart the parent, which is failing to reap children.

causes.cause: A supervisor restarts it.
causes.fix: Stop the unit rather than the process.

causes.cause: Blocked on an unreachable NFS server.
causes.fix: Restore the server, or force-unmount. This is the most common cause of permanent D state.

causes.cause: It is a kernel thread.
causes.fix: Kernel threads cannot be killed. Names in square brackets in ps are kernel threads.

verify: The process is gone and does not return.
Whatever blocked it was resolved.
No new zombies accumulate.

title: Hostname does not resolve on this machine
summary: Name lookups fail locally even though the network is fine.

steps.title: Test resolution through the full name service stack
steps.look: getent follows nsswitch.conf exactly as applications do. dig and nslookup bypass it, which is why they can succeed while your app fails.

signals.means: Not resolved through the normal path.
It resolves. The application's failure is something else.

steps.title: Check the resolver configuration
steps.look: The nameserver entries. A 127.0.0.53 entry means systemd-resolved is the local stub, and the real servers are one layer further in.

steps.title: Check the lookup order
steps.look: The hosts line decides whether files, DNS or mDNS are consulted and in what order. A missing dns entry means DNS is never used at all.

steps.title: Query the nameserver directly
steps.look: Whether the configured server can answer. An answer here with getent failing points at nsswitch rather than DNS.

causes.cause: resolv.conf has no usable nameserver.
causes.fix: Add one, or fix whatever manages the file. NetworkManager and systemd-resolved both rewrite it.

causes.cause: systemd-resolved is the stub and its upstreams are wrong.
causes.fix: Check resolvectl status for the real upstream servers.

causes.cause: The hosts line omits dns.
causes.fix: Add it. Without it, only /etc/hosts is consulted.

causes.cause: A search domain rewrites the query.
causes.fix: Use a fully qualified name with a trailing dot to bypass the search list.

causes.cause: UDP 53 is blocked.
causes.fix: Check egress. Some networks force DNS through a specific resolver.

causes.cause: Resolution works; the application fails for another reason.
causes.fix: Check its own configuration and any proxy settings.

verify: getent resolves the name.
The application connects.
It survives a network restart.
escalate: resolv.conf and the nsswitch hosts line
Whether dig against the configured server answers

title: User cannot log in
summary: Authentication fails or the session closes immediately after a successful login.

steps.title: Check the account's status
steps.look: Locked state and expiry dates. An expired account or password blocks login even with correct credentials.

signals.means: The password is locked.
An expiry date is set. Check whether it has passed.

steps.title: Check the login shell
steps.look: The last field. /sbin/nologin or /bin/false means authentication succeeds and the session immediately ends, which looks like a login failure.

signals.means: The account has no interactive shell by design.

steps.title: Read the authentication log
steps.look: The precise reason. PAM states whether it was the password, the account state or an access restriction.

steps.title: Check whether a lockout policy is blocking them
steps.look: Failed attempt counts. Repeated failures can lock an account for a period, and the message given to the user does not say so.

causes.cause: The password is locked.
causes.fix: passwd -u to unlock. Find out why it was locked first.

causes.cause: The account or password expired.
causes.fix: chage to extend. Password expiry policies catch service accounts routinely.

causes.cause: The shell is nologin.
causes.fix: Intentional for service accounts. Change it only if interactive access is genuinely needed.

causes.cause: Too many failed attempts.
causes.fix: faillock --reset. Then find out what was retrying with a bad password.

causes.cause: access.conf or a PAM rule denies them.
causes.fix: Read auth.log. It names the module that denied.

causes.cause: The home directory does not exist.
causes.fix: Login can fail or behave oddly. Create it with the right ownership.

verify: The user logs in.
The session stays open.
auth.log shows a clean accepted entry.
